title: Could quantum computing threaten Israel's biotechnology edge?
excerpt: Opinion: As quantum computing advances, increasingly accessible molecular simulations could allow global pharmaceutical giants to challenge Israel’s growing edge in AI-driven drug discovery, forcing its biotech sector to rethink how it stays competitive
content:
Opinion: As quantum computing advances, increasingly accessible molecular simulations could allow global pharmaceutical giants to challenge Israel’s growing edge in AI-driven drug discovery, forcing its biotech sector to rethink how it stays competitive

Related Topics

A recent report by Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) warned that advances in quantum technologies could eventually threaten Israel’s qualitative military advantage as sophisticated computing capabilities become more widely accessible.

However, a similar question deserves attention in biotechnology, where computational capabilities are becoming increasingly important to the discovery of new medicines. Could quantum computing eventually weaken Israel’s competitive position in drug discovery by making some of its emerging technological strengths less distinctive?

Israel has developed a growing presence in AI-assisted drug discovery, building on its expertise in computing and biological research. According to the 2025–26 life-sciences industry report produced by the Israel Advanced Technology Industries Association and the Israel Innovation Authority, approximately 30 Israeli companies operate at the intersection of AI and drug development. Their activities reflect a growing opportunity for Israel to compete in drug discovery by using computational methods to identify and optimize potential drug candidates.

Yet some of the scientific challenges these companies are addressing could eventually be affected by quantum computing. Today, AI and conventional computing help researchers predict molecular properties, evaluate potential interactions with biological targets and prioritize compounds for experimental testing. However, accurately calculating certain molecular interactions remains difficult because the behavior of electrons and chemical bonds can be exceptionally complex, creating problems that future quantum computers may be better equipped to solve.

This is where the potential competitive threat emerges. If quantum computing eventually makes sophisticated molecular calculations more accurate, efficient and widely accessible, some of the computational capabilities that help distinguish AI-driven drug discovery could become less exclusive. Quantum computing would not necessarily replace AI, but it could improve particular calculations used to evaluate and optimize compounds, potentially allowing biotechnology companies worldwide to perform tasks that currently require considerable computational expertise and resources.

This possibility is already being explored experimentally. On November 17, the Israeli quantum software company Classiq, which Intel agreed to acquire in October, announced research with Japanese drug developer Shionogi using quantum algorithms to study molecular interactions relevant to drug discovery. The researchers tested their approach through simulations and actual quantum hardware, although the work did not demonstrate a practical advantage in discovering medicines. Nevertheless, it illustrates how international drug developers are beginning to investigate quantum computing for scientific problems directly relevant to identifying and optimizing compounds.

The broader concern is that countries with larger biotechnology industries, research budgets and experimental infrastructure could eventually combine widely available quantum-assisted calculations with resources that Israel cannot match at the same scale. If that happens, Israel might remain highly competitive in developing computational technologies while finding that its existing expertise offers less differentiation in drug discovery, particularly against companies capable of applying advanced calculations across extensive experimental programs.

None of this is inevitable, particularly because quantum computing has yet to demonstrate a reliable practical advantage in drug discovery. Although Israel has established capabilities in AI-assisted drug discovery and quantum software, this does not mean its biotechnology companies are already routinely combining the two.

The opportunity is therefore to investigate where quantum-assisted methods could genuinely improve existing computational approaches and prepare Israeli drug-discovery companies to adopt them as their value becomes clearer.

Nevertheless, just as Israel is considering whether quantum technologies might alter its military advantage, its biotechnology sector should examine how they could change the foundations of competition in drug discovery. The potential risk is not that Israel will lose its ability to discover medicines, but that competitors may gain access to computational capabilities that narrow the advantages Israel is seeking to build.

  • Professor David Adler is chief scientific and medical officer of the PATHORA Institute of Pathology & Tissue Medicine.
